newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco wheat imports seen declining in Jan-June.
newsitem.headline: Morocco wheat imports seen declining in Jan-June.

text.p: New customs duties imposed by the government on soft wheat will lead to a drop in tonnage in the first half of 1997, Moroccan traders said on Thursday.
A cabinet meeting presided over by Prime Minister Abdellatif Filali on Wednesday approved a law raising customs duties on imported soft wheat to 59 percent from 35 percent.

"We should wait and see when the law will be applied because the cabinet did not specify the date of its application," a Casablanca-based trader said, adding, "One thing is sure is that the imported amount is going to fall in the first half of 1997."
The government decree is expected to be published soon in the official bulletin when it will become law, an official said.
"The new increase is in fact a simple adjustment in line with the drop in wheat prices on the international market," a spokesman at the Trade Ministry told Reuters.

Morocco, which complies with World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules, had set a custom duty of 35 percent using as a base figure a price of 1,300 dirhams ($146) for each tonne of imported wheat. That duty had now been changed to 59 percent, the spokesman said.

Morocco plans to import one million tonnes of soft wheat in the 1996/97 season, starting last July, the agriculture ministry has said. Late last year, an official with the cereal traders' association said Morocco had imported more than half a million tonnes of wheat since May 1.
The government's new initiative would affect private importers while the state-owned Office National des Cereales et Legumineuses (ONICL) would continue to import, a market analyst said.
The trade ministry said the move was aimed at "protecting the small farmers and the local industry because competition is becoming very tough."
Morocco in May 1996 launched a policy of gradual liberalisation for commodities over a four-year period to comply with agreements signed earlier with the WTO.

"During the first six months of liberalisation, the prices on the domestic market of cereals were disrupted...In the period of August, September and October the prices dropped by 20 percent due to massive imports from abroad," an analyst said.

The country, which has had a cycle of droughts followed by good rains since 1990, also plans to safeguard what the authorities describe as a strategic stock of wheat estimated at between 2.5 and 3.0 million tonnes.
In 1995, Morocco suffered a catastrophic drought and had to import an estimated 2.55 million tonnes of cereals, including wheat.
